def: The 2×2 table of true positives, false positives, false negatives, and true negatives at a given threshold. Every classification metric is a ratio of its cells.
A positive case the model correctly flagged.
A negative case the model wrongly flagged: a false alarm.
A positive case the model missed.
A negative case the model correctly left alone.
The score cutoff above which a classifier predicts positive. Moving it trades false positives for false negatives.
TP / (TP + FP): of the items flagged, the share that were truly positive.
TP / (TP + FN): of the truly positive items, the share that were flagged. Also called sensitivity or true positive rate.
TN / (TN + FP): of the truly negative items, the share left alone. Recall for the negative class; one minus the false positive rate.
FP / (FP + TN): the share of negatives wrongly flagged. The x-axis of an ROC curve.
(TP + TN) / n. Misleading when one class is rare, because it mostly measures the common class.
Harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR / (P + R). High only when both are high; ignores true negatives.
Weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall; β > 1 weights recall more, β < 1 weights precision more.
The mean of recall and specificity. 0.5 is chance at any prevalence.
Correlation between predictions and labels using all four confusion-matrix cells, from −1 to +1. A strong single-number summary under imbalance.
Agreement between two raters corrected for the agreement expected by chance: (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e).
The share of items that are truly positive. Precision and PR-AUC depend on it; recall, FPR, and ROC-AUC do not.
Recall plotted against false positive rate as the threshold sweeps from high to low. Each threshold is one point.
Area under the ROC curve; the probability a random positive scores higher than a random negative. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
Precision plotted against recall as the threshold sweeps. Sensitive to prevalence.
Area under the precision–recall curve, usually computed as average precision. Its chance baseline equals the prevalence.
Unweighted mean of a metric across classes, so every class counts equally.
Mean of a per-class metric weighted by class support. Can hide poor performance on rare classes.
A metric computed from counts pooled across classes. In single-label multiclass, micro-F1 equals accuracy.
Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: of items given 70% confidence, about 70% should be positive.
Mean squared error between predicted probabilities and 0/1 outcomes. A proper scoring rule; lower is better.
Weighted average gap between confidence and accuracy across confidence bins. Depends on the number of bins.
Dividing logits by a single learned constant on held-out data to fix calibration without changing rankings.
Letting a model abstain on low-confidence cases and measuring error only on the cases it answers.
Error rate on answered items as a function of the share of items answered (coverage).
(c_FP·FP + c_FN·FN) / n: the average cost per decision once the two errors are priced.
The specific threshold, and resulting precision and recall, at which a classifier is actually deployed.
Using a language model to grade or compare model outputs. A classifier that must itself be validated against humans.
A pairwise judge's tendency to prefer the response shown in a particular position. Controlled by judging both orderings.
A judge's tendency to score longer responses higher regardless of quality.
A judge scoring outputs from its own model family more favourably.
The agreement two humans reach on the same labels. No judge or classifier can meaningfully exceed it against human labels.
The difference between a judge's pass rate and humans' on the same items. A generous judge inflates every absolute number while still ranking models correctly.
